4.text: unions. In ancient times this form of marriage was obviously a union between

5.text: the members of a related group. In course of time, other friendly persons

6.text: began to be included in the union. The rite accompanying the formation of

7.text: group-marriages reflects such an origin, for it is intended to give the union

8.text: the character of a tie between relatives. The persons concerned make sacri-

9.text: fices and anoint themselves with blood, first in one camp, and then in the

10.text: other. After that they are considered as belonging to one fireside, as do the

16.text: The older people, however, were reluctant to enter the group-union with

17.text: young people, especially if the latter were single. The mixing of ages in the

18.text: group-marriage is not approved of. If a married man, on the other hand,

19.text: has no children, but desires to have some, he is anxious to make a union

20.text: with a strong single man. The aversion to including bachelors in the mar-

21.text: riage-group is primarily based on the absence of reciprocity. The bachelor

22.text: gains from entering the union, but gives nothing in return.

23.text: The inmates of one and the same camp are seldom willing to enter into

24.text: a group-marriage, the reason obviously being that the reciprocal use of wives,

25.text: which in group-marriage is practised very seldom, is liable to degenerate into

26.text: complete promiscuity if the members of the group live too close together.

27.text: However, many exceptions occur to both rules. As an illustration of group-

28.text: marriage between a married couple and a bachelor, the following union, which

29.text: I observed in one of the camps, may be cited. A young Chukchee, married

30.text: but childless, served as a shepherd in the herd of a rich reindeer-breeder.

31.text: In the marriage-union was included another shepherd, also young but single,

32.text: who was a Tungus. All three lived in one tent. When the Chukchee
